messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Community Organizer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 49

# The Weight of the Wreckage

Marcus is a 63-year-old Māori man who has spent the better part of three decades organizing communities across Auckland — rallying neighbors around housing rights, coordinating youth programs, building the kind of trust between people that takes years to grow. He is known in his circles as someone who shows up, who remembers names, who can hold a room together when everything feels like it's falling apart. What most people in those rooms don't know is that for the past two years, Marcus has been quietly falling apart himself.

In the winter of 2022, Marcus was driving home from a late community meeting when a truck ran a red light and struck his car on the driver's side at full speed. The car was pushed across two lanes and into a barrier. He remembers the sound — a tearing, crushing sound he describes as the world being crumpled like paper — and then a strange, suspended silence before the pain arrived. He was trapped in the vehicle for nearly forty minutes. He broke three ribs, fractured his left wrist, and sustained a laceration across his forehead that required surgery. He was told afterward that another few inches and he would not have survived.

The physical injuries healed within months. What didn't heal was harder to name at first. In the weeks after the accident, Marcus told himself he was simply tired, that his body needed rest. But sleep became something he dreaded. When he did sleep, he was back in the car — not always reliving the crash exactly, but existing inside the terror of it, the certainty that he was about to die. He would wake with his heart hammering, sometimes shouting, sometimes just rigid and soaked in sweat, unable to remember for a moment where he was or whether he was still alive.

Driving became impossible. He sold his car within three months, telling colleagues it was a practical decision, that public transport was better for the environment. But the truth was that sitting in any moving vehicle — even a bus — sent his body into a state of alarm he couldn't reason his way out of. He would grip the seat, watch every intersection, count the seconds between lights. Some days he got off the bus several stops early and walked, just to make the feeling stop.

His work began to suffer in ways that embarrassed him. Marcus had always prided himself on his presence — his ability to listen, to hold space for others' pain. Now he found himself sitting in community meetings, nodding along, while some part of his mind was elsewhere, scanning for danger he couldn't identify. He lost the thread of conversations. He forgot follow-up calls he had promised to make. He became irritable in ways that surprised even him — snapping at a young volunteer over something trivial, then sitting in his car afterward, ashamed, replaying the moment over and over.

His marriage had ended several years before the accident, and he lives alone now in a small flat in Tāmaki. The solitude, which once felt manageable, has become heavier. He avoids the intersection where the crash happened, which means adding fifteen minutes to any journey through that part of the city. He avoids news stories about road accidents. He has stopped watching certain films. He has constructed, without fully realizing it, an elaborate geography of avoidance around his daily life.

What brings Marcus to therapy now is not one dramatic moment of crisis but a slow accumulation of losses — the friendships he's let thin out, the meetings he's stopped attending, the sense that the man he was before that night in 2022 is becoming harder to remember. He sits in the chair with his hands folded in his lap, composed and articulate, and says that he doesn't want to be the kind of person who lets something like this define him. Then, almost involuntarily, he glances toward the window, as though checking that the street outside is still safe.
